opus-5.5.text:
When I say "cleanly," I mean doing research where you actually know *why* something worked. That sounds obvious, but in reinforcement learning, especially RL on top of large language models, it's surprisingly hard.

The problem is that the system has so many moving parts. There's the base model, the pretraining data, the prompts, the reward model or verifier, the hyperparameters, the sampling temperature, the length of the rollouts, and a dozen implementation details in the training framework. You get a result, the score goes up, everyone is happy, but if you're honest you often can't say which of those things caused it. Maybe it was your new algorithm. Or maybe it was a small change in how you filtered the data, or the reward was being hacked, or the evaluation set overlapped with something the model had already seen.

So doing it cleanly means a few things for me.

First, control your variables. Change one thing at a time and keep strong, fair baselines. If you compare your method against a baseline you didn't tune very carefully, the comparison doesn't mean much.

Second, be suspicious of your own gains. In RL the model is an optimizer, and it will find any shortcut in your reward. If the number goes up very fast, my first reaction shouldn't be excitement. It should be to look at the samples and check whether the model learned the behavior I wanted or just exploited the reward.

Third, separate what you learned about the method from what you learned about the setup. A lot of RL papers end up being true only for one model, one dataset, one scale. A clean result tells you something that transfers, or at least tells you honestly where it stops working.

And finally, it's a kind of discipline in how you think. It's tempting to keep adding tricks until the curve looks good. Clean research means sometimes removing things, simplifying until you find the minimal setup where the phenomenon still shows up. When you get there, you actually understand it, and that understanding is worth much more than one more point on a benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response favors simplifying the setup and removing tricks, but it does not question whether algorithms beyond basic policy gradient are necessary.

r002.rationale: It mentions implementation details as one source of confounding, but does not frame algorithm choice as a tradeoff between efficiency gains and infrastructure difficulties.

fable-5.1.text:
When I say "cleanly," I'm really talking about isolating the variable you actually care about. A lot of RL work, especially on language models now, mixes everything together at once: a new environment, a new reward design, a new training trick, a huge model, and then a result comes out and you genuinely don't know which part did the work. The paper says "our method improves reasoning," but maybe it was the data, maybe it was the prompt, maybe it was the fact that you ran three times as many rollouts.

So "cleanly" for me means a few things. First, start with the simplest possible setup where the question is still meaningful. If I want to know whether a model can learn to plan from reward alone, I don't need a frontier-scale model and a messy real-world task. I need a task where I can enumerate what "good planning" looks like, where I can read the trajectories by hand, and where if something fails I can tell you exactly why it failed.

Second, change one thing at a time. That sounds obvious, but in practice it's expensive, because each variant costs compute and people are under pressure to show a big number. But if you don't do it, you end up with a lot of folklore. Everyone "knows" that some trick helps, but nobody can reproduce it under controlled conditions.

Third, be honest about the prior. In RL for language models, the model has already absorbed an enormous amount from pretraining. So when you see learning, you have to ask: did RL teach the model something new, or did it just sharpen a behavior that was already there? Those are very different claims, and a clean experiment is designed so you can distinguish them. That's actually why I like thinking about agents and environments so much. The environment defines what counts as real learning. If you design it carefully, the answer becomes clear. If you design it carelessly, you can convince yourself of almost anything.

And honestly, the last part is a kind of discipline about what you report. If a result only shows up with one random seed, or only on one benchmark, I'd rather say that than dress it up. Clean research is slower, but it compounds. You build a small set of things you actually believe, and then the next experiment stands on something solid instead of on a pile of guesses.

r001.rationale: The response advocates simple setups and controlled experiments, but does not question whether RL algorithms more complex than basic policy gradient are necessary.

r002.rationale: It discusses complexity in experiments and compute costs, but does not frame algorithm choice as a tradeoff between efficiency gains and infrastructure difficulties.

astra-6.text:
I think “cleanly” means making it clear what question you’re trying to answer and what your experiment actually demonstrates. With reinforcement learning, you can change the model, the data, the reward, the environment, and the amount of compute, and then get a better result. But which change was responsible? Did you learn something about reinforcement learning, or did you build a stronger system through a lot of engineering?

So I would start with a specific hypothesis, keep the comparison controlled, and use the simplest setting that still captures the problem. You also need a strong baseline. If a simpler method gets the same result with the same resources, that’s something you should acknowledge.

It doesn’t mean engineering is unimportant. It means separating “we made this work” from “we understand why this works.” Both are valuable, but a clean piece of research makes that distinction explicit.

r001.rationale: The response recommends simple settings and strong baselines, but does not specifically question whether algorithms more complex than basic policy gradient are necessary.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes engineering from understanding and mentions resource-controlled comparisons, but does not describe a tradeoff between efficiency gains from complex algorithms and their infrastructure difficulties.

sol-6.1.text:
By “cleanly,” I mean setting up the research so that you can understand why something works. You have a clear question, a well-defined environment, and an evaluation that actually tests the capability you care about. Then you try to isolate the contribution of reinforcement learning: is the model learning a better strategy, or is the improvement coming from more sampling, better data, or some detail of the reward?

For example, if a model gets a higher reward, that alone doesn’t tell you it has become more capable. It might have found a shortcut in the evaluator. You want to check whether the improvement carries over to new problems, and compare against a strong baseline with a similar compute budget.

So “clean” doesn’t necessarily mean simple or small. It means the evidence supports the claim you’re making. Ideally, even if the result is negative, you’ve learned something clear about the problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses isolating RL’s contribution and validating results, but does not question whether algorithms beyond basic policy gradient are necessary.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute budgets and evaluation, but does not frame algorithm choice as a tradeoff between efficiency gains and infrastructure difficulties.
